items.title: Michael White interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 10, 2025
items.q: I notice with Kenny... he would – sometimes they would puff their cheeks out a little bit. Unfortunately I didn’t learn how to do that and I don’t know how to do that.

ctx.x: I don't know if this is a myth in my head, but when I was watching, just this morning I was watching a video of him and he would do a certain amount of, I call it “finger whacking.” And I know Kenny Davern would do this too, like he’d lift certain fingers up and really almost percussively play the instrument that way. And I was thinking well a classical clarinet teacher would not appreciate that. If they had a ruler they might slap your wrist. But I’m wondering if that physicalness of the finger movement is part…

I believe that it is. I believe every physical – slight movements of the lip, the cheeks, all of those things affect the tone and the sound. I notice with Kenny, and I noticed with George Lewis in videos and stuff, he would – sometimes they would puff their cheeks out a little bit. Unfortunately I didn’t learn how to do that and I don’t know how to do that. But I also tried different things. Because what you realize is you want the instrument to be like your voice and an expression of how you feel so you don’t…

Were you surprised along the way in your path through jazz history – I was, one time was reading a book and it mentioned one of those earlier New Orleans musicians and that they were a barber. And I think I was naïve enough to think that all those fellows, all they did was just play music. And I don’t even know if that’s possible then – it’s hard now but was it possible then?
